# Organobismuth Compounds as Aryl Radical Precursors via Light-Driven Single-Electron Transfer

**Authors:** Nicholas D. Chiappini; Eric P. Geunes; Ethan T. Bodak; Robert R. Knowles

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton NJ, 08544.

## Abstract

A light-driven method for the generation of aryl radicals from triarylbismuth(III) and (V) reagents is described. Aryl radical generation is proposed to occur through ligand-assisted mesolytic cleavage of an organobismuth(IV) intermediate generated from either oxidation of BiIII or reduction of BiV. This mode of aryl radical generation is demonstrated to be compatible with a range of bimolecular radical arylations, including hydroarylation of electron-deficient olefins and arylation of diboronates, disulfides, sulfonyl cyanides, phosphites and isocyanides. The intermediacy of an aryl radical is supported by radical trapping and radical clock experiments, and BiIV-aryl mesolysis is supported computationally.

## Abstract

Recent progress in organobismuth chemistry has led to attendant advances across main group catalysis, organometallic chemistry, and organic synthesis.ch Organobismuth compounds were first reported in the 1850s,1–3 and numerous oxidation states have since been studied.5–9 For example, triarylbismuthines, which are organobismuth(III) compounds, have been successfully employed as nucleophiles in transition metal-catalyzed cross-coupling with a range of sp2 and sp3 electrophiles and are capable of transferring all three aryl groups (Figure 1a).4–9 In contrast, aryl organobismuth(V) compounds are best known for their use as electrophilic aryl transfer reagents via ligand coupling (Figure 1b).10–17 More recently, bismuth redox catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for achieving diverse polar and radical reactivity as exemplified by the works of Cornella and Lichtenberg (Figure 1c).18–29 In addition to these thermal processes, ultraviolet, and near-visible irradiation can also directly cleave weak Bi–C bonds to generate aryl or alkyl radicals (Figure 1d).30–33 Recently, several interesting examples of photochemical bismuth mediated reactivity, including SET, Giese additions and oxidative addition have been described.18,34–36

Despite these advances, the chemistry of bismuth(IV) remains largely underexplored. This is due in large part to the propensity of BiIV to disproportionate into BiIII and BiV species. 37–39 Moreover, invocations of BiIV in the chemical literature are chiefly resigned to high energy systems, such as γ-ray irradiation of aqueous solutions of BiIII.37,38 A notable exception comes from Fuchigami, who investigated the electrochemical oxidation of triarylpnictines (N, P, As, Sb, Bi).40 While electrolysis of PPh3, AsPh3, and SbPh3 cleanly produced the corresponding Ph3PnVX2 species, NPh3 and BiPh3 instead yielded products consistent with both radical and cationic intermediates. From this, Fuchigami proposed the formation of a BiIV radical cation, analogous to well-known triarylaminium radical cations. In rationalizing the formation of biphenyl, Fuchigami invoked mesolytic cleavage of Ph3Bi•+ to form Ph• and [Ph2Bi]+ (Figure 1e). Based on our prior work with aminium radical cations we were intrigued by this proposal for aryl radical generation and questioned if similar BiIV based reactivity could instead be accessed through light-driven single electron transfer (SET) with either BiIII or BiV species. 41,42

We hypothesized that the low concentration of BiIV generated by photocatalyst-mediated SET would abrogate competitive disproportionation into BiIII and BiV species, thereby allowing for generation of aryl radicals from stable precursors (Figure 1f).

Our initial explorations paired Ph3Bi (Ep/2 = 1.08 V vs Fc+/Fc (MeCN)) with an excited state photooxidant [Ir(dF(CF3)ppy)2(5,5’-d(CF3)bpy)]PF6 (E1/2(*IrIII/IrII) = 1.28 V vs Fc+/Fc (MeCN)) under blue light (456 nm) irradiation in the presence of an electron-deficient olefin acceptor in PhCF3 (Table 1). We were pleased to observe formation of phenylalanine derivative 1a in 48% yield. Exploration of alternative solvents revealed pivalonitrile (tBuCN) to be superior for aryl transfer (entries 1–5), affording 1a in 70% yield. In these reactions yields were calculated with respect to bismuth as at the outset of optimization, it was unclear how many aryl radicals could be generated from each Ar3Bi, thus in cases where more than one aryl radical is generated yields may exceed 100% for a maximum of 200% if 1a is fully consumed. Product formation was exclusively observed when excited-state photooxidants43–45 capable of oxidizing Ph3Bi were employed (entries 1–12). Notably, no aryl transfer was observed when using weakly oxidizing photocatalysts with triplet energies exceeding that of Ph3Bi (56 kcal/mol;31 entry 9, 10), suggesting electron-transfer, rather than energy transfer, is the operative mechanism of substrate activation. We selected organic photocatalyst 4-BrCzIPN (entry 12) as the model catalyst due to its low cost and comparable redox properties to the aforementioned Ir-photocatalyst. No hydroarylation was detected in the absence of irradiation or photocatalyst (Entry 13, 14). Use of anhydrous tBuCN greatly diminished the yield of hydroarylation (entry 15), with chiefly alkene polymerization observed. In contrast, tBuCN that was used as received and stored on the benchtop proved optimal. As such, we presumed that adventitious water serves as the terminal proton source following reduction of the nascent α-carbonyl radical by the reduced photocatalyst. This hypothesis was supported by recovery of reactivity when 5.0 equivalents of H2O were added to anhydrous tBuCN (entry 16). Water as terminal proton source was supported by attenuation of the α-H signal in 1a when D2O was added to anhydrous tBuCN (see Supporting Information). Additionally, increasing alkene loading to 5.0 equivalents (entry 17) only marginally improved the yield at the expense of significant alkene oligomerization. While triphenylbismuthine was found to be superior to other heavy triarylpnictines for hydroarylation, Ph3As afforded 1a in 60% yield (entries 18, 19). Neither the stibine or arsine afforded hydroarylation product 1a in the absence of photocatalyst and due to their toxicity, we opted to forgo further investigation for the present study in favor of the bismuthine.

As the hypothesis for aryl radical generation involves mesolysis of Ph3Bi+•, we drew inspiration from the work of Feinberg and Dinnocenzo46–51 examining nucleophile-assisted mesolytic cleavage of aryl trimethyl silane, germane, and stannane radical cations. Alcohols and nitriles were found to be optimal nucleophiles for driving Group 14 mesolysis, thus we hypothesized alcohol additives might behave similarly for arylbismuthine mesolysis in addition to serving as a terminal proton donor (Scheme 1).

When a 10:1 v/v mixture of tBuCN and methanol was used as solvent, yields improved to 82% (entry 2). We then examined methanol and other alcohols at reduced loading and found 1.0 equivalent of benzyl alcohol afforded the desired product in 115% yield with respect to 1.0 equivalent Ph3Bi (entry 4). Substituted benzyl alcohols and other aliphatic alcohols proved inferior at 1.0 equivalent loadings (Table S3, see supporting information).

With optimal conditions in hand, we then evaluated the scope of hydroarylation with Ph3Bi and a range of electron-deficient olefins (Figure 2a). We found that acceptor olefins bearing pyridines, purines, and benzimidazoles afforded hydroarylated products in synthetically useful yields, as did dehydroamino acid derivatives, benzylidene malononitriles, vinyl phosphonates, and vinyl amides (1a–8a). Observation of product 8a derived from dimethylacrylamide was surprising, as reduction of the α-radical formed upon aryl radical addition is expected to be endergonic (est. Ep/2 < –1.37 V vs Fc+/Fc (MeCN))52 with respect to the reduced state of the photocatalyst (E1/2(PC/PC•–) = –1.46 V vs Fc+/Fc (CH2Cl2))53. We hypothesized that this may be due to a lowering of the reduction potential of the nascent α-carbonyl radical adduct by association with cationic [Ph2Bi]+ produced via BiIV mesolysis. To test this, we prepared α-diphenylbismuthino methyl phenyl sulfone and found its oxidation potential to be Ep/2 = 0.93 V vs Fc+/Fc (MeCN). This is in stark contrast to the reduction potential of the α-sulfone radical as measured by Bordwell (Ep/2 = –0.53 V vs Fc+/Fc (DMSO))54 and suggests significant attenuation in reduction potential can be conferred via association with [Ph2Bi]+ (See Supporting Information). Unactivated alkenes were also extensively explored with a variety of bismuthines and hydrogen atom donors and showed moderate success, albeit with complex reaction mixtures (Table S1, See Supporting Information). As such, we instead focused our attention toward electron-poor alkenes.

After examining the reaction scope with electron-poor olefins, we explored aryl transfer from bismuthines to several other reaction partners including diboronates (9a), disulfides (10a–14a), sulfonyl cyanides (15a), and phosphites (16a), with omission of benzyl alcohol and use of anhydrous tBuCN as solvent (Figure 2b). In these cases, we hypothesize that turnover is achieved by reduction of the radical leaving group (RS•, Ts•, etc.) or [Ph2Bi]+. Following this, we explored the triarylbismuthine scope using P(OEt)3 as a model aryl radical acceptor given its efficacy with Ph3Bi (Figure 2c). Bismuthines with a range of simple substitution patterns including electron-donating groups, electron withdrawing groups, and ortho-alkylation proved amenable to aryl transfer (16b–16h). To accommodate the use of more complex aryl fragments, we demonstrated that 9-arylated bismafluorenes ([FlBi]Ar) can serve as suitable scaffolds for selective transfer of the monodentate aryl group (16c’, 16h’).

The proposed BiIV intermediate could also be generated from reduction of BiV species by a more reducing photocatalyst. We found that with 4-CzIPN (E1/2(PC*/PC+) = –1.12 V vs Fc+/Fc (MeCN))38 as a photocatalyst and Ph3BiF2 (Ep/2 = –1.32 V vs Fc+/Fc (MeCN)) ([BiF2]a) as an aryl radical source, net oxidative arylations were observed for various radical acceptors including biaryl isocyanides (17a), aniline-derived vinyl amides (18a), and sulfonamides (19a) (Figure 2d). Ph3BiF2 was selected for this purpose as Ph3BiCl2 was found to have background photolytic activity in the absence of a photocatalyst, likely via a radical chain mechanism (Table S2, see Supporting Information).

This method provides a flexible platform form aryl radical generation via either oxidative (from Ar3BiF2) or reductive (from Ar3Bi) quenching of a photocatalyst. Common aryl radical precursors 55such as aryl halides56–60, sulfonium salts61–63, iodonium salts64, diazonium salts65–68, boronic acids69–71 carboxylic acids36,72–74 instead are either strictly oxidative or reductive. Reductive precursors such as iodonium, sulfonium, and diazonium salts typically need either oxidative turnover (limiting compatibility with hydroarylation), while oxidative precursors often require strong stoichiometric oxidants and are incompatible with reductive turnover.

Preliminary mechanistic experiments were consistent with aryl radical generation via mesolysis of a Bi(IV) intermediate (Scheme 2). Addition of TEMPO to hydroarylation reactions resulted in complete suppression of formation of 1a, and PhOTEMP (20a) was instead isolated in 28% yield. Additionally, when the reaction was conducted with TEMPO in the absence of 1a, the PhOTEMP adduct was isolated in 70% yield. Notably, no background reactivity was observed between Ph3Bi and TEMPO in the absence of light and photocatalyst (Scheme 2a). Arylations of 1 with homoleptic o-allyloxy and o-isobutoxy phenylbismuthines ([Bi]i; [Bi]j) afforded products of 5-exo-trig cyclization and 1,5-hydrogen atom transfer, respectively, followed by Giese addition (Scheme 2b, 2c). These observations indicate the generation of aryl radical intermediates under the optimized hydroarylation conditions. To further investigate the thermochemistry of the proposed Bi–C mesolysis from the BiIV radical cation, we computed bond dissociation free energies (BDFEs) for the Bi–C bond in Ph3Bi•+ with no solvation and explicit solvation with tBuCN (Scheme 2d). Explicit solvation was modeled through binding anti- to one of the Bi–Ph substituents in analogy to binding of nucleophiles to the aryl-tetrel antibonding orbital in the work from Dinnocenzo et al. and Xiao et al.46,50 In the gas phase, the Bi–C BDFE was calculated to be 25.6 kcal/mol, a substantial drop from the 47.5 kcal/mol of Ph3Bi.31,75 Upon coordination of tBuCN or BnOH, the gas-phase BDFE was found to decrease markedly to 6.0 kcal/mol and 11.0 kcal/mol, respectively, supporting potential nucleophile-assisted mesolysis.

Together, these findings corroborate the observed reactivity and support the feasibility of mesolytic generation of aryl radicals from BiIV in analogy to similar behavior observed with group 14 elements.46,50 In light of these observations, we propose the following general mechanism for hydroarylation (Scheme 2e): after initial electron transfer from triphenylbismuth to the excited-state photocatalyst, the nascent BiIV intermediate undergoes mesolytic cleavage assisted by tBuCN, yielding an aryl radical and a cationic BiIII complex. Subsequent aryl radical Giese addition to a radical acceptor results in a stabilized alkyl radical which can then be successively reduced by the photocatalyst and protonated by benzyl alcohol to afford the hydroarylated product. As successful hydroarylation was observed even in cases where reduction of the α-carbonyl radical is endothermic, electron transfer from the reduced photocatalyst may be assisted by coordination with the cationic BiIII complex. The fate of the bismuth byproduct is less clear; in most reactions, a heavy black precipitate of elemental Bi is observed and efforts to isolate and characterize potential bismuth-containing byproducts were thus far unsuccessful.

In summary, we present a light-driven method mediated by single-electron transfer for the generation of aryl radicals from bench-stable organobismuth(III) and organobismuth(V) compounds via formation of transient organobismuth(IV) intermediates. The intermediacy of aryl radicals is supported by experimental observations and computational investigation of the bond dissociation energies in organobismuth(IV) intermediates, supporting the invocation of this uncommon oxidation state. We hope that access to alternative aryl radical generation methods and ability to access the underexplored BiIV oxidation state will provide opportunities for the development of new catalytic systems for aryl transfer and bond formation.
